subject: physics
title: Errors, uncertainties, precision and accuracy
key_idea: No measurement is exact. Random errors scatter readings, and systematic errors shift them all one way. Every result carries an uncertainty, which can be written as an absolute or percentage value and combined when quantities are added, multiplied or raised to powers.

blocks.text: Errors are the differences between a reading and the true value. They fall into two types with different effects.

items.meaning: An error that makes repeated readings scatter unpredictably above and below the true value.
An error that shifts every reading by the same amount or the same proportion, in the same direction.
A systematic error where the instrument reads a non-zero value when it should read zero.

rows: reaction time, reading a scale by eye
zero error, a clock that runs fast
calibrating, or correcting for the zero error

items: A zero error shifts every reading by the same amount, so the whole graph line is shifted.
On a graph of y against x, a systematic error often shows as an intercept that is not where it should be.
A large scatter of points about the best-fit line shows random error.
Random errors scatter readings and are reduced by taking a mean.
Systematic errors (including zero errors) shift every reading and are not removed by averaging.

blocks.text: Precision and accuracy are different things. A measurement can have one without the other.

items.meaning: How close a measurement is to the true value.
How close repeated measurements are to each other.
The smallest change an instrument can detect.

items: Readings of 9.8, 9.9 and 9.8 for a true value of 9.81 are both precise and accurate.
Readings of 8.2, 8.2 and 8.3 for a true value of 9.81 are precise but not accurate. A systematic error is likely.
Random error reduces precision. Systematic error reduces accuracy.
An instrument with a smaller resolution allows more precise readings.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeats to each other.
A precise set of readings can still be inaccurate.

blocks.text: An uncertainty shows the range in which the true value is likely to lie. It can be given in three ways.

blocks.label: Percentage uncertainty
where: absolute uncertainty is in the same unit as the measured value
fractional uncertainty is the same ratio without × 100

items: Write a result as 20.0 ± 0.5 cm: the absolute uncertainty is 0.5 cm.
Its fractional uncertainty is 0.5 ÷ 20.0 = 0.025, and its percentage uncertainty is 2.5%.
For a single reading, take the uncertainty as half the resolution at the least, and often the full resolution.
For repeated readings, use half the range (largest − smallest) as the uncertainty in the mean.

rows: multiply the percentage uncertainty by n

items: For a length of 10.0 ± 0.1 cm and a width of 5.0 ± 0.1 cm, the area uncertainty is 1% + 2% = 3%.
For a radius with 2% uncertainty, the area (πr²) has 4% uncertainty.
Subtracting two close values makes the percentage uncertainty much larger.

diagram.alt: A practice question. Find the percentage uncertainty in the area of a rectangle.
diagram.question: A rectangle has sides of {a} ± {da} cm and {b} ± {db} cm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in its area.

items: Percentage uncertainty = absolute uncertainty ÷ value × 100.
Add absolute uncertainties for sums and differences; add percentages for products and quotients.

blocks.text: An error bar shows the uncertainty in a plotted point. The spread of bars tells you how well the line is known.

items: Draw an error bar as a line through the point, of length equal to the uncertainty either side.
Error bars can go on the x values, the y values or both.
The best-fit line should pass through (or very near) all the error bars.
The worst line is the steepest or shallowest line that still passes through all the error bars.

items.text: Draw the best-fit line and the worst acceptable line.
Calculate the gradient of each: Δy ÷ Δx using a large triangle.
The uncertainty in the gradient is the difference between the best and worst gradients. Do the same for the intercept.

items: Error bars show the uncertainty in each plotted point.
The difference between the best and worst line gradients gives the uncertainty in the gradient.

checks.q: A student measures a current with an ammeter that reads 0.04 A with nothing connected. State the type of error and describe how to deal with it.
checks.a: It is a zero error (a systematic error). Subtract 0.04 A from every reading, or reset the meter to zero.

checks.q: A pendulum period is T = 1.50 ± 0.03 s. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in T².
checks.a: % uncertainty in T = 0.03 ÷ 1.50 × 100 = 2%. For T², multiply by 2, giving 4%.

checks.q: Explain the difference between a precise set of readings and an accurate one.
checks.a: Precise readings are close together (small scatter); accurate readings are close to the true value. Readings can be precise but all shifted by a systematic error, so not accurate.

items.meaning: How close repeated measurements are when the same person uses the same method and apparatus.
How close measurements are when a different person or different apparatus is used.

items: Use resolution as well as precision and accuracy to describe the quality of a measurement.
Not every point on a graph needs an error bar. Some points may have none.
Find the uncertainty in the gradient and in the intercept of a straight-line graph from the best and worst lines.
Apply the limits of measurement to a real experiment: say which instrument limits the precision and how that affects the percentage uncertainty in the result.
Choose the improvement that reduces the largest percentage uncertainty, such as a larger measured quantity or a more precise instrument.
Explain the effect of each error on the result, for example that a zero error shifts every value by the same amount.
Assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute uncertainties (for sums and differences) or percentage uncertainties (for products and quotients).
For a power, add the percentage uncertainty once for each factor: x² has twice the percentage uncertainty of x.

blocks.label: Percentage difference
blocks.formula: percentage difference = (|value 1 − value 2| ÷ mean of the two values) × 100%
where: value 1 and value 2 are the two results being compared, in the same unit

items: Combine uncertainties for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and raising to powers, as in the table above.
Percentage errors in apparatus: a ruler marked in mm has an uncertainty of about ±0.5 mm, so a short length has a large percentage uncertainty.
Give margins of error as a range, such as 4.8 ± 0.2 N.
An elementary knowledge of error bars is enough. A full statistical treatment is not needed.
